title: Modal verbs
description: Kan, vill, ska, måste, får and bör with a bare infinitive, their negatives and their past forms.

guide.summary: Swedish modal verbs work like English can and must: they are followed by the plain infinitive, with no att. This page covers their forms, vill ha for wanting things, permission with får, the difference between måste and behöver inte, where inte goes, and the past.

sections.title: Six modal verbs
sections.text: Modal verbs say whether you can, want, will, must, may or ought to do something. In the present they have one short form for every person; only får and bör end in -r.
steps: Find the modal you need from its meaning.
Use the same present form for every person: jag kan, vi kan.
Do not add -r or -ar, except to få, which is får.
watch: Viller, kanar and måstar do not exist.
Får keeps its ring: far means father.

sections.title: No att after a modal
sections.text: After a modal the next verb is the plain infinitive, with nothing in between. English can swim has no to either; Swedish extends that to all six verbs, even where English says want to.
steps: Put the modal second, after the subject.
Follow it directly with the infinitive.
Leave out att, and keep the second verb free of tense endings.

examples.en: We are going to eat dinner now.

watch: Jag kan att simma is wrong.
Only the modal shows tense: jag vill läsa, never jag vill läser.

sections.title: Vill ha: wanting a thing
sections.text: Vill always needs a verb after it. To want a thing, Swedish says want to have: vill ha.
steps: Ask: is the wanted thing an object or an action?
For an object, say vill ha plus the thing.
For an action, say vill plus that verb.

examples.en: The children want to go home now.

watch: Jag vill kaffe is wrong: a verb is missing.

sections.title: Får: may, be allowed to
sections.text: Får asks or gives permission. Får inte is a ban: must not.
steps: To ask, put får first: Får jag ...?
For a ban, say får inte.
watch: English must not becomes får inte, not måste inte.

sections.title: Måste and behöver inte
sections.text: Måste means must or have to. To say there is no need, use behöver inte. Måste inte is heard in speech, but it is ambiguous, and many read it as a ban.
watch: Avoid måste inte: it is unclear.

sections.title: Inte after the modal
sections.text: In a main clause the modal is the second element, and inte follows it directly, before the infinitive.
steps: Then the infinitive and the rest.
watch: Not jag inte kan, not jag kan komma inte.

sections.title: The past: kunde, ville, skulle, fick
sections.text: Each modal has its own short past form. Only the modal changes; the infinitive stays. For had to, Swedish usually says var tvungen att, and here att is needed, because tvungen is an adjective, not a modal.
steps: Find the modal in the table.
Keep the next verb in the infinitive.

examples.sv: Han skulle komma, men han blev sjuk.
examples.en: He was going to come, but he got ill.

examples.sv: Jag var tvungen att jobba igår.

watch: Var tvungen att keeps att; the real modals never do.

steps: Find the modal from its meaning.
Use one form for every person.
Find the past form in the table.
Keep the next verb in the infinitive.

exercises.hint: Modal verbs do not take the usual -r in the present.
exercises.feedback: The present of kunna is kan for every person.
exercises.explanation: Jag kan: one short form, no -r.

mistakes.why: Kunna is irregular: its present is not built from the infinitive with -ar.
Modal verbs drop the normal present -r; this form does not exist.
Kunna is the infinitive. After jag you need the present form.

exercises.hint: Short form, same for all persons.
exercises.feedback: The present of vilja is vill.
exercises.explanation: Hon vill: vilja has the irregular present vill, with no -r.

mistakes.why: Vilja does not follow the -ar pattern; its present is a short irregular form.
There is no -er on this verb in the present: modal verbs end without -r.
Ville is the past, wanted. The task asks for the present.

exercises.hint: Få is the one modal here that keeps the -r.
exercises.feedback: Få gets -r like an ordinary verb: får.
exercises.explanation: Vi får: same form for every person, with -r.

mistakes.why: Få is the infinitive. The present needs its -r ending.
Far without the ring means father, or travels. The ring over the a is part of this verb.
Fick is the past, was allowed or got. The task asks for the present.

exercises.hint: Present of kunna, one short form for every person.
exercises.feedback: Kunna in the present is kan.
exercises.explanation: Hon kan laga mat: kan, then the infinitive laga.

mistakes.why: Kunna does not take -ar: its present is irregular and short.
The infinitive cannot be the main verb after hon; it needs the present form.
Kunde is the past, could. The sentence is about now.

exercises.hint: Böra means ought to. Which form is the present?
exercises.feedback: Böra has the present bör, with no extra ending.
exercises.explanation: Du bör sova mer: you ought to sleep more.

mistakes.why: Böra does not take -ar. Like most modals, its present is short.
Böra is the infinitive. After du you need the present form.
There is no -er on this verb; the present is short.

exercises.hint: Look at the modal verb. Does it have an ending it should not have?
exercises.feedback: Vilja is vill in the present, with no -er.
exercises.explanation: Erik vill komma på festen: vill is the present for everyone.

mistakes.why: The verb is unchanged: viller is not a Swedish form.
Ville is the past, wanted. Keep the sentence in the present.

answers: Erik vill att komma på festen.
mistakes.why: The ending is fixed, but att has crept in. A modal is followed directly by the infinitive.

exercises.hint: After a modal, the next verb is the plain infinitive.
exercises.feedback: No att and no present ending after kan.
exercises.explanation: Jag kan simma: I can swim.

mistakes.why: English can swim has no to, and neither does Swedish: kan is followed directly by the verb.
Simmar is a present form. Only the modal carries the tense; the second verb stays in the infinitive.
Simmat is the supine, used after har. After kan you need the dictionary form.

exercises.hint: Wants to speak: Swedish leaves out the to.
exercises.feedback: After vill comes the bare infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Hon vill prata svenska: no att after vill.

mistakes.why: English says wants to speak, but Swedish puts nothing between vill and the verb.
Pratar is the present. The modal vill already carries the tense, so the second verb stays in the infinitive.
Pratade is the past. The second verb never carries tense after a modal.

exercises.instruction: Write the right form of äta.
exercises.hint: After ska, the verb stays as it is in the dictionary.
exercises.feedback: Ska is followed by the bare infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Vi ska äta middag nu: we are going to eat dinner now.

mistakes.why: Äter is the present form. After ska the verb is not conjugated.
No att after ska: the modal is followed directly by the verb.
Åt is the past. The second verb never carries tense after a modal.

exercises.hint: One small word is too many.
exercises.feedback: Modal verbs are never followed by att.
exercises.explanation: Jag kan simma: kan goes straight to the infinitive.

mistakes.why: The sentence is unchanged. Att, the to of English, never stands after a modal.
Att is gone, but now the second verb has a present ending. Only the modal shows the tense.
Two problems: the extra word and a present ending on the second verb.

exercises.hint: English to has no tile to match.
exercises.feedback: Leave out the att tile.
exercises.explanation: Jag vill sova: vill followed directly by the infinitive.

mistakes.why: Att does not follow a modal. Vill takes the infinitive directly.
Sover is the present form. After vill the verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.source: We are going to eat lunch.
exercises.hint: Plans: ska plus the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Ska, then the dictionary form of äta.
exercises.explanation: Vi ska äta lunch: ska carries the plan, äta stays in the infinitive.

mistakes.why: Going to is ska alone. No att comes between ska and the verb.
After ska the verb is the infinitive, not the present.
Swedish does not use gå for future plans; ska does that job.

exercises.instruction: Add vill (want) and write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Put vill after jag and change läser.
exercises.feedback: After vill, the verb goes back to the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Jag vill läsa en bok: vill takes the present, läsa stays in the dictionary form.

mistakes.why: Vill now carries the present tense, so the other verb has to drop its -er.

answers: Jag vill att läsa en bok.
mistakes.why: No att after a modal.
The modal comes in second place, straight after the subject, with the infinitive after it.

exercises.hint: Wanting a thing, not an action.
exercises.feedback: To want a thing, say vill ha.
exercises.explanation: Jag vill ha kaffe: literally I want to have coffee.

mistakes.why: Ha is right, but att never follows a modal.
Har is the present form. After vill the verb is the infinitive.
Dricker is a present form. After vill you would need the infinitive, and wanting a thing is the usual phrase here.

exercises.hint: Here the children want to do something: go home.
exercises.feedback: Vill ha is only for things. For an action, use that action’s verb.
exercises.explanation: Barnen vill gå hem: vill plus the infinitive gå.

mistakes.why: Vill ha means want a thing. Home is not something you have here; it is where they want to go.
Går is the present. After vill the verb stays in the infinitive.
No att after a modal.

exercises.hint: You are offering a thing to drink.
exercises.feedback: With a thing, vill needs ha.
exercises.explanation: Vill du ha te eller kaffe? Do you want tea or coffee?

mistakes.why: Har is the present. After vill the verb is the infinitive.
No att after a modal.
Hade is the past. After vill the verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.hint: Swedish adds a verb English leaves out.
exercises.feedback: Want a thing: vill ha.
exercises.explanation: Jag vill ha kaffe. En kaffe, one cup, is also fine.

mistakes.why: Vill on its own needs a verb after it. To want a thing, add the verb for having.
No att after vill.
After vill the verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.hint: Something is missing between vill and the thing.
exercises.feedback: A thing wanted needs vill ha.
exercises.explanation: Jag vill ha en glass: I want an ice cream.

mistakes.why: The sentence is unchanged. Vill needs a verb after it.

answers: Jag vill att ha en glass.
mistakes.why: No att after a modal.
The verb after vill must be in the infinitive.

exercises.hint: Wanting a thing takes two verbs in Swedish.
exercises.feedback: Vill, then ha in the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Hon vill ha en hund.

mistakes.why: Har is the present. After vill, ha stays in the infinitive.
A verb is missing: to want a thing, Swedish says want to have.

exercises.hint: This is a rule: it is forbidden.
exercises.feedback: Not allowed is får inte.
exercises.explanation: Man får inte röka här: smoking is not allowed here.

mistakes.why: Behöver inte means there is no need to. A sign about smoking is a ban, not a choice.
Vill inte means does not want to. A rule is about what is allowed.
Måste inte is not how Swedes write a ban. It sounds like there is no obligation, which is the opposite of a rule.

exercises.instruction: Write the verb that asks permission.
exercises.hint: You are asking permission.
exercises.feedback: May I is får jag.
exercises.explanation: Får jag sitta här? May I sit here?

mistakes.why: Without the ring, far means father. Permission needs the å.
Måste jag means must I, which asks about an obligation, not permission.
Ska jag means shall I, an offer or a plan, not asking permission.

alternatives.message: Fine in everyday speech, but it asks if it is possible. For permission, Swedish prefers the få form.

exercises.hint: Permission: the modal from få comes first in the question.
exercises.feedback: Questions put the verb first: får jag.
exercises.explanation: Får jag sitta här? Kan jag sitta här? is also heard, but får is the polite way to ask permission.

mistakes.why: A yes/no question starts with the verb.
No att after a modal.
Far without the ring is father. Permission needs the å.

exercises.hint: Must not means not allowed.
exercises.feedback: Use får inte for a ban.
exercises.explanation: Du får inte röka här: must not is not allowed in Swedish.

mistakes.why: Must not in English is a ban. Swedish says it with not allowed; måste inte is read as no need to.
Behöver inte means you do not need to, which is not a ban.
Inte goes straight after the modal, before the infinitive.

exercises.instruction: Make it a ban: add inte.
exercises.hint: Inte goes straight after the modal.
exercises.feedback: Add inte after får.
exercises.explanation: Du får inte parkera här: you must not park here.

mistakes.why: Inte comes after the modal, not after the infinitive.
In a main clause the verb stays second; inte follows it.
The task is to forbid it. Keep får and add the negation.

exercises.source: We are allowed to swim here.
exercises.hint: Allowed to: one modal, no to.
exercises.feedback: Får, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Vi får simma här.

mistakes.why: No att after a modal.
Måste is must. Being allowed is a different verb.

exercises.source: Du ____ inte jobba idag. Det är söndag.
exercises.hint: It is Sunday: there is no need to work.
exercises.feedback: Do not have to is behöver inte.
exercises.explanation: Du behöver inte jobba idag: you do not have to work today.

mistakes.why: Får inte means you are not allowed to. Nobody forbids working on Sunday; there is just no need.
Måste inte is heard in speech, but it is unclear (in Finland Swedish it can mean a ban). For no need, use the verb that means need.
Kan inte means you are not able to. The point is that there is no need.

exercises.hint: It is a must: I have to call.
exercises.feedback: Must is måste.
exercises.explanation: Jag måste ringa mamma nu: I must call mum now.

mistakes.why: This verb never changes its ending: one form for every person.
There is no -er on this verb; it has one fixed form.

exercises.hint: Do not have to: no need.
exercises.feedback: Behöver inte, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Du behöver inte betala: there is no need for you to pay.

mistakes.why: Får inte is a ban: you are not allowed to pay.
Inte goes straight after the first verb.

alternatives.message: Understood and common in Sweden, but behöver inte is the clearest way to say no need: Du behöver inte betala.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error. The speaker means there is no need to wait.
exercises.source: Du måste inte vänta på mig.
answers: Du behöver inte vänta på mig.
exercises.hint: The speaker means: no need to wait.
exercises.feedback: For do not have to, swap the modal.
exercises.explanation: Du behöver inte vänta på mig: you do not have to wait for me.

answers: Du måste inte vänta på mig.
mistakes.why: Unchanged. Måste inte is unclear; it can sound like a ban.

answers: Du får inte vänta på mig.
mistakes.why: Får inte forbids waiting, which is not what the speaker means.

answers: Du behöver inte att vänta på mig.
mistakes.why: The modal is right, but drop att.

exercises.instruction: Change it to mean I don't have to.
exercises.hint: Say there is no need.
exercises.feedback: Måste becomes behöver inte.
exercises.explanation: Jag behöver inte städa idag: I do not have to clean today.

mistakes.why: Får inte means you are not allowed. The task is about no need.
Inte goes straight after the modal.

alternatives.message: Common in speech, but behöver inte is clearer: Jag behöver inte städa idag.

exercises.hint: Must is måste, with the infinitive straight after.
exercises.feedback: No att after måste.
exercises.explanation: Jag måste jobba idag.

mistakes.why: No att after a modal.
After måste the verb is the infinitive.

exercises.hint: Inte sits right after the modal.
exercises.feedback: Modal, inte, infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Jag kan inte komma i morgon: I cannot come tomorrow.

mistakes.why: In a main clause the verb comes second, before inte.
Inte does not go after the infinitive; it follows the modal.
The order is right, but att never follows a modal.

exercises.hint: The negation goes between the modal and the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Inte follows the modal.
exercises.explanation: Hon vill inte äta fisk: she does not want to eat fish.

mistakes.why: Nej is the answer no. Inside a sentence, use the negation word.
Aldrig means never, which is stronger than the word asked for.
The negation is right, but att never follows it before the infinitive here.

exercises.hint: Check the order of kan and inte.
exercises.feedback: The modal stays second; inte comes after it.
exercises.explanation: Jag kan inte komma.

mistakes.why: Unchanged. In a main clause inte follows the verb.
Inte comes before the infinitive, not after it.
Inte does not start the sentence before the subject here.

answers: Han ska inte jobba i morgon.
exercises.hint: Put inte right after the modal.
exercises.feedback: Ska, then inte, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Han ska inte jobba i morgon.

answers: Han ska jobba inte i morgon.
mistakes.why: Inte goes before the infinitive, straight after ska.

answers: Han inte ska jobba i morgon.
mistakes.why: The verb stays second in a main clause, inte after it.

exercises.hint: Modal, inte, infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Inte follows kan.
exercises.explanation: Vi kan inte simma.

mistakes.why: The modal stays second; inte comes after it.
No att after a modal.

exercises.hint: No do in Swedish: just put inte after the modal.
exercises.feedback: Vill inte, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Hon vill inte dansa.

mistakes.why: Inte follows the verb in a main clause.
No att after a modal.
Inte comes before the infinitive.

exercises.hint: The past of kan ends in -de.
exercises.feedback: Kunna: kan, kunde.
exercises.explanation: Jag kunde: I could.

mistakes.why: Kunna is irregular; the past is short.
Kan is the present. The task asks for the past.
Kunnat is the supine, used after har.

exercises.hint: Past of vill: one letter changes.
exercises.feedback: Vilja: vill, ville.
exercises.explanation: Han ville: he wanted.

mistakes.why: Vilja is irregular; the past is short.
Vill is the present.
Velat is the supine, used after har.

exercises.hint: The past of få looks nothing like the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Få: får, fick.
exercises.explanation: Vi fick: we were allowed, we got.

mistakes.why: Få is irregular; its past is a different word.
Får is the present.
Fått is the supine, used after har.

exercises.hint: The past of ska is a longer word.
exercises.feedback: Ska: skulle.
exercises.explanation: De skulle: they were going to, they should.

mistakes.why: Ska is irregular; there is no -de form.
Ska is the present.
That is the supine, almost never used.

exercises.hint: Yesterday: past of kan.
exercises.feedback: Kan in the past is kunde.
exercises.explanation: Igår kunde jag inte sova: yesterday I could not sleep.

mistakes.why: Kan is the present, but igår puts this in the past.
The infinitive cannot be the main verb here.
Kunna is irregular; this form does not exist.

exercises.source: Han ____ komma, men han blev sjuk.
exercises.hint: A plan in the past that did not happen.
exercises.feedback: Past of ska: skulle.
exercises.explanation: Han skulle komma, men han blev sjuk: he was going to come, but he got ill.

mistakes.why: Ska is the present. Blev shows this is in the past.
Ska has no -de past.
Ville is a past, but att never follows a modal.

exercises.hint: Had to in the past: be forced to, with att.
exercises.feedback: Var tvungen att means had to.
exercises.explanation: Förra veckan var jag tvungen att jobba varje dag. Here att is needed, because tvungen is not a modal verb.

mistakes.why: Tvungen is an adjective, not a modal, so the verb after it needs att.
After a time phrase at the start, the verb comes second, before the subject.
Måste is a modal, and modals never take att.

answers: Jag var tvungen att jobba igår.
Igår var jag tvungen att jobba.
Jag var tvungen att arbeta igår.
exercises.hint: Had to: var tvungen att.
exercises.feedback: Var tvungen att, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Jag var tvungen att jobba igår. Måste also works in the past, but var tvungen att is clearer.

mistakes.why: Tvungen is not a modal, so att is needed.
Swedish does not use ha for must.

exercises.hint: Only the modal changes; the infinitive stays.
exercises.feedback: Vill becomes ville.
exercises.explanation: Jag ville äta.

mistakes.why: Only the modal carries the tense.
The modal carries the tense; the infinitive stays.
